concerns.text: The "first arrival" target (week when cumulative count reaches the 5th observation) is confounded with observer effort. Complete-checklist filtering (FR-001) controls checklist quality, not spatial heterogeneity in sampling intensity: heavily-birded cells reach the 5th detection earlier regardless of biology, so the model may learn observer-density geography rather than phenology. The spec excludes low-effort cells (<10 obs) but has no design (effort covariate, per-cell checklist normalization, or spatial random effect) to control high-effort bias in the target itself. This threatens the core claim that temperature/NDVI predict migration timing.

The Diebold-Mariano test is applied to grid-cell prediction errors that are spatially autocorrelated (neighboring 0.5° cells share weather and arrival dates) and pooled across a single test year (2022). DM assumes (approximately) uncorrelated loss differentials; treating thousands of spatially dependent cells as independent samples will drastically inflate significance for the p<0.05 acceptance criteria in US-2/US-3. A block/spatial bootstrap or HAC correction over space is needed, or the test must be applied at a coarser independent unit.

Requiring "a mean absolute SHAP value difference of at least 10% between the two features" as an acceptance scenario bakes the empirical finding into the spec. Whether temperature vs NDVI differ by ≥10% is exactly the research question; making it a pass/fail criterion turns a falsifiable hypothesis into a design requirement and invites result-driven tuning. State it as a hypothesis to be reported, not an acceptance threshold.

FR-004 says the test split is "subsequent period" (vague, and data runs to 2023) while US-2 and SC-001 pin it to 2022. Align FR-004 to the explicit 2022 test year (and state how 2023 data, if ingested per FR-001's 2015–2023 range, is used) to avoid ambiguity about the evaluation set.
